newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels said to be advancing on Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels said to be advancing on Kisangani.

text.p: Zairean rebels advanced on several fronts on Monday towards the northeastern capital of Kisangani, the centre for army resistance against them, a regional military source said.

Rebel chief Laurent Kabila says his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire is aiming at Kisangani, a commercial centre, key port on the Zaire river and Zaire's third largest city.

A regional military source, who has closely monitored the rebellion in the east since it started in October, said: "Our information is they are advancing on several fronts towards Kisangani. It appears to be a show of strength by the rebels."
"It is also a tactic to disorganise the government forces and their allies already panicking in Kisangani," he added.

It was not clear how close to Kisangani the rebels had advanced. The rebels said they captured the town of Lubutu, about 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani, on Saturday. A straight road joins the two towns.
Rebels said their forces advancing from the east were closer to Kisangani than the fighters who took Lubutu, but they gave no details.
Kabila on Sunday dimmed hopes for a ceasefire in the war by rejecting South African and U.S. pressure to make a deal.
In his clearest public statement about secret talks in South Africa last week, he said he refused to sign an agreement to end the war to topple ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Kabila told a news conference in the eastern border city of Goma his forces were making steady progress on the battlefield and had captured Lubutu, seven km (four miles) from Tingi Tingi, the site of the largest refugee camp in Zaire.

He appealed to the United Nations to help 170,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees who fled Tingi Tingi last week in fear of an imminent rebel attack. But he insisted there could be no truce without direct negotiations between the rebels and Mobutu.
In Nairobi, an exiled Rwandan Hutu lobby group appealed on Monday to the international community to end the suffering of the refugees, most of whom fled to Zaire from Rwanda in 1994.

"Recent developments in the fighting in eastern Zaire have worsened the already precarious situation of the refugees," the Rally for the Return of Democracy and Refugees to Rwanda (RDR) said in a statement.
"They are condemned to death in the camps (in eastern Zaire). Those who are still able to walk are likely to die of fatigue, starvation and poor health care," said the statement.
Kabila says rebels overran Tingi Tingi camp on Saturday, prompting the refugees along with Rwandan Hutu former troops and militiamen who have fought alongside Zairean troops to flee.
The former Rwandan troops and militiamen had a leading role in the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda in 1994 and refuse to return home.
Brenda Barton of the U.N. World Food Programme said on Monday that 309 refugees from Tingi Tingi arrived in Kisangani but they had apparently left the camp before most others.
Aid workers said the refugees from Tingi Tingi were rying to reach Kisangani or nearby Ubundu town.
"From the air it apeared that there were no more refugees left at Tingi Tingi," an aid worker said.

The aid workers were quoting colleagues who flew over the Tingi Tingi area when they were evacuated by plane from the town of Bunia. They said the plane was shot at with automatic weapons over the camp.
U.N. agencies pulled their last foreign workers out of their headquarters in Kisangani on Saturday.
